sections.h2: Before you agree to sell: Point of Sale
sections.html:
In Euclid, the order of operations is fixed by law. Before signing a sale agreement, the owner obtains a Point of Sale application and a Certificate of Code Compliance from the Housing Department, and the buyer receives the certificate. Chapter 1759 of the city's codified ordinances makes it unlawful to agree to sell or convey a dwelling without one in hand.

After you buy the application, a city inspector goes through the house and the lot. The resulting list of known violations drives your next move: repair the items, or let the buyer take them on. Start this step before you list, since the paperwork shapes both your price and your timeline.

sections.h2: Point of Sale fees and deadlines
sections.html:
Chapter 1759 spells out the terms in plain numbers, and every seller gets the same ones.

Euclid Point of Sale rules, Codified Ordinances Chapter 1759
SituationRule
Application fee$225.00, plus $35.00 per unit for buildings with more than three units
Life of the certificateSix months, and no new inspection if the property sells in that period
Renewal after no sale50% of the original fee, if the owner reports in writing within 30 days after expiration
Elderly owners with the county homestead exemptionFee drops to $100.00, except for transfers caused by the owner's death
Violations still open at saleBuyer files an Assumption application and corrects them within 180 days of transfer
Sheriff's sale purchase of a one, two or three family homeBuyer purchases the application within ten days, corrects violations within 180 days

Owners of one or two family homes who sell and relocate within Euclid can apply for a rebate of the $225.00 fee when they buy another one or two family residence as their primary home. Assumed violations still open after 180 days can lead to prosecution under Section 1703.99.

The Building, Housing and Nuisance Department takes calls Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., at (216) 289-2700. Extension 3908 covers Point of Sale and assumptions, 3904 residential permits, 3905 rental requirements, 3906 tall grass and yard debris, and 3903 vacant property registration. Send permit applications as email attachments to buildingandhousing@cityofeuclid.gov, because the office can't accept photos of forms.

  • Ask about the Point of Sale inspection before you list so the violation list is in your hands when buyers call.
  • Ask whether a vacant house must be registered with the city. Chapter 1763 ties exemptions to a current Point of Sale inspection and a for sale status.
  • Fence and shed questions go to the same office. The city caps combined garage and shed area at 696 square feet and allows no shed taller than ten feet.

The city's Housing Accessibility and Rehabilitation Grant Program excludes problems found in a Point of Sale inspection, so don't plan on it to pay for sale repairs.

sections.h2: Owning in Euclid: what buyers weigh
sections.html:
Euclid is an inner ring Cleveland suburb on Lake Erie, in Cuyahoga County. Population is 47,962 for July 2025, down 3.5 percent from the April 2020 base. Owners live in 46.4 percent of homes, so rentals are a large part of the market.

  • Median value of an owner occupied home: $126,500
  • Median gross rent: $1,025
  • Households: 22,433, averaging 2.16 people
  • Median household income: $50,285

The city sits in the Lake Erie Snowbelt, so lake squalls test roofs, gutters and driveways every winter, and buyers inspect those items closely. Euclid City Schools is the public district. A rental owner who sells should know that Ohio Revised Code 5323.02 requires owners of residential rental property to file ownership details with the county Fiscal Officer.

sections.h2: Recording the deed in Cuyahoga County
sections.html:
The Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office Transfer and Recording division, at 2079 E. Ninth Street, 4th floor, Cleveland, phone 216-443-2060, handles the deed. Every transfer needs either a DTE 100 Statement of Value and Receipt or a DTE 100-EX exemption form. Office hours are Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with recording until 4:00 p.m.

Recording costs $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each page after. Preparing a deed counts as the practice of law, and county staff can't advise on it, so a title company or attorney normally drafts it.

sections.h2: The state form and the city form
sections.html:
Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 asks sellers of one to four unit homes to deliver a signed property disclosure form to buyers. A Euclid seller usually completes both that state form and the city's Point of Sale paperwork.

They do different jobs. The city's certificate reports code violations found by an inspector. The state form is your own statement about the condition of the house. Neither replaces the other, and buyers will read them side by side.

sections.h2: Selling a Euclid house with violations
sections.html:
Open violations don't kill a sale. They change who does the work. With the Assumption application, the buyer agrees to correct the listed items within 180 days of transfer, and those items stay open until then. A buyer who plans to renovate anyway may welcome that arrangement, and it lets you skip repairs you wouldn't have recovered in the price.

Repairing first suits a seller who wants a wider pool of buyers, especially buyers using a lender, who may balk at a long violation list. Compare the cost of the repairs with the discount a buyer asks for. If a certificate lapses after six months with no sale, you can renew it for 50% of the original fee by reporting in writing within 30 days of expiration.

sections.h2: A step by step plan for a Euclid sale
sections.html:
First, call extension 3908 and buy the Point of Sale application. Second, let the inspector visit and read the violation list carefully. Third, decide which items you will repair and which the buyer will assume, keeping the 180-day correction window in mind. Fourth, complete the state disclosure form and gather repair receipts.

Once you have a contract, hand the certificate to the buyer and have the deed prepared by a title company or attorney. The deed goes to the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office with a DTE 100 or DTE 100-EX form, and recording follows. If the property sold within the six months of the certificate, no new inspection is needed.

A cash buyer will often accept the house with violations, which removes the repair step, though the Assumption application and the 180-day correction window still apply to that buyer. Ask each buyer for a written price, closing date and cost split, and compare offers side by side.

faqs.q: Does Euclid require an inspection before I sell?
faqs.a: Yes. Chapter 1759 requires a Point of Sale application and a Certificate of Code Compliance before you agree to sell, and the buyer must receive a copy. The application fee is $225.00.

faqs.q: What if my Euclid house fails the Point of Sale inspection?
faqs.a: You can fix the violations, or the buyer can take them on by filing an Assumption application and correcting them within 180 days of the transfer. Call extension 3908 at (216) 289-2700 for the steps.

faqs.q: How long does a Euclid Certificate of Code Compliance last?
faqs.a: Six months. If the property sells during that period, no new Point of Sale inspection is required for the sale.

faqs.q: Can a senior pay less for the Euclid Point of Sale application?
faqs.a: Yes. The fee falls to $100.00 for elderly Euclid homeowners who receive the Cuyahoga County homestead exemption, except when the property transfers because the owner died.

faqs.q: Where is a Euclid deed filed?
faqs.a: With the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office Transfer and Recording division in Cleveland, along with a DTE 100 or DTE 100-EX form. Call 216-443-2060 to confirm what your document needs.
